Paper vs. Film Labels: A Substrate Buyer's Guide

Paper wins on cost and aesthetics in dry, indoor conditions; film wins wherever moisture, cold, chemicals, abrasion, or sunlight appear.

Decide by environment and required service life first, then match adhesive and topcoat, then compare price per label. Paper is the correct engineering answer for dry ambient warehousing, short shelf-life SKUs, and corrugated cases. Film — BOPP, PET/polyester, or PP/PE — is the correct answer wherever the product sees freezer or cooler cycling, wash-down or solvent contact, frequent handling, outdoor storage, or a multi-year service life. Arrow Systems’ ArrowJet Aqua 330R and ArrowJet UV 330H are digital press platforms built to run mixed paper and film portfolios on the correct substrate per SKU. The right choice depends on your specific journey environment, not a single blanket substrate decision across the whole portfolio.

Key Takeaways

  • Label substrate selection is an environment decision with a price attached — profile temperature, moisture, chemical exposure, handling, and service life before comparing cost per label.
  • Paper fails through fiber saturation, edge lift below freezing, condensation cycling, ink smear, solvent attack, abrasion, and UV embrittlement — the mechanism determines whether the fix is facestock, adhesive, or topcoat.
  • Film substrates (BOPP, PET/polyester, PP/PE) remove the fiber-saturation problem entirely because there is nothing to saturate, but the adhesive class still has to match the job.
  • Facestock, adhesive, and topcoat function as one system — changing one element means re-checking the other two, not swapping a single component in isolation.
  • Digital inkjet behaves differently on each substrate: porous paper absorbs aqueous ink and dries by penetration, while non-porous films need a receptive topcoat, compatible ink chemistry, or both.

Where Paper Labels Excel: Cost, Aesthetics, and Low-Demand Environments

Paper is not a compromise material — in dry, indoor, short-service-life conditions, it is the correct engineering answer.

This guide is for operations, engineering, QA, and packaging teams who own label specs and get the call when labels come off in the field. Most substrate decisions get made twice: once on price, then again after a label peels in a freezer case, smears after a caustic wash-down, or scuffs unreadable in transit.

Lowest cost per label

Paper facestocks are typically the least expensive pressure sensitive label stock, and the cost gap widens on large-format case and carton labels.

Printability and aesthetics

Uncoated, matte, and textured papers deliver the natural, non-plastic look many food, beverage, and specialty brands want. Ink sits well and dries fast.

Recyclability and repulpable options

Paper facestocks and repulpable case-label constructions can simplify corrugated recycling streams, producing more sustainable pressure sensitive labels than a laminated film construction. Verify claims with your material supplier and your own waste program.

Conformability on rough surfaces

On fibrous or uneven substrates such as corrugated, paper often lays down better than a stiffer film.

Best-fit conditions: dry ambient warehousing, short shelf-life or fast-turn SKUs, corrugated shipping cases, dry-goods cartons, hardware and dry-fill packaging, and pharmacy or dispensing labels that live indoors for a defined period.

Where Paper Labels Fail: Cold, Wet, Chemical, and High-Abrasion Environments

Paper failures start in wet conditions — the mechanism determines whether the fix is a facestock, adhesive, or topcoat change.

Fiber saturation

Paper is a fiber matrix. Absorbed water swells fibers, destroys tensile strength, and produces wrinkling, tearing, and delamination. It shows up first on cold storage labels used on iced protein cases and condensation-heavy cooler storage.

Edge lift and adhesive stiffening

Below freezing, many general-purpose adhesives lose tack as they stiffen. Paper’s own dimensional movement adds stress at the perimeter — the result is classic cold storage failure: corners curling off a frozen case within days.

Condensation cycling

Product moving freezer to dock to cooler to truck sees repeated wet and dry cycles. Each cycle drives moisture under the edges and weakens the bond further.

Ink smear and barcode dropout

After a wash-down cycle, ice slurry, or hose contact, unprotected paper can bleed or abrade. A dropped barcode or lot code stalls scanning at receiving and creates traceability gaps that require manual resolution.

Solvent and cleaner attack

Caustic CIP chemistry on dairy and beverage lines, plus solvents and lubricants on chemical pails, drums, and totes, will soften paper and lift adhesive well before they affect a film.

Abrasion loss

Hand-handled totes, returnable containers, automotive parts bins, and pallet-to-pallet transit rub print off paper quickly.

UV exposure

Paper labels on equipment, drums, or inventory in yard or outdoor storage fade and embrittle in sunlight. A film facestock with UV-stabilized ink and a protective topcoat produces UV resistant labels that hold their color and bond for years in the same yard or outdoor storage.

The downstream cost is where the savings disappear: relabeling labor, held shipments, rejected loads, and repeat scanning problems that nobody traces back to the substrate spec.

Film Labels: BOPP, Polyester, and Polypropylene Options and Their Properties

Film substrates replace the fiber matrix with a continuous polymer film — there is nothing to saturate, which explains most of the durability gap.

The decision to move to film usually comes down to moisture, chemical exposure, abrasion, or a service life measured in years rather than weeks.

BOPP (biaxially oriented polypropylene)

The workhorse film. A BOPP label is available in white, clear for a no-label look, or metallized, commonly in the 2 to 3 mil range of BOPP label material — confirm against your supplier’s data sheet. It offers strong moisture resistance, good clarity, moderate chemical resistance, and a cost position modestly above paper. Common uses: bottles, jars, tubs, cold-chain packaging, and household or personal care containers.

PET (polyester)

The step up. A PET label, often sold simply as a polyester label, handles higher temperatures, resists solvents and abrasion better than BOPP, and holds dimensional stability under stress, often at a thinner caliper for comparable stiffness. Used for chemical drum and tote identification, rating and asset plates, tamper-evident constructions, and parts that see heat or aggressive cleaners.

PP and PE (polypropylene and polyethylene)

Softer and more conformable films. A PP label — often specified as polypropylene label material — is the right choice for squeezable bottles, irregular geometry, and containers that flex in use, where a stiffer PET label would tunnel or pop off.

Adhesive class matters as much as facestock

Waterproof labels still fail if you pair a premium facestock with a general-purpose adhesive. Match the label adhesive to the job: permanent all-temp or freezer-grade for direct-to-frozen application, wash-off for returnable glass, high-tack for low-surface-energy plastics such as HDPE and PP pails.

Topcoats and finishing as durability multipliers

Receptive topcoats make non-porous films printable with the right ink chemistry, and laminates or UV varnishes add chemical, scuff, and light protection on both paper and film constructions. Arrow’s label finishing systems apply cold lamination and protective topcoats inline, regardless of which substrate or press produced the roll.

How to Decide Between Paper and Film for Your Specific Application

A repeatable substrate selection workflow beats SKU-by-SKU guessing: profile the environment, match materials, then test before buying.

Step 1: Profile the full journey environment

Temperature range and rate of change, moisture and condensation exposure, chemical and cleaner contact, handling and abrasion frequency, expected service life, and outdoor exposure.

Step 2: Identify the application surface

Corrugated, HDPE pail, coated glass, stainless steel, powder-coated metal, or flexible film. Texture and surface energy drive adhesive choice.

Step 3: Define the readability requirement

Human-readable only, scanned 1D barcode, or 2D code, plus how long it must stay scannable and at which points in the journey.

Step 4: Match facestock, adhesive, and topcoat as one system

Change one element and re-check the others — a substrate upgrade with the wrong adhesive still fails.

Step 5: Run a pre-qualification test

Freeze and thaw cycling, water immersion plus rub, cleaner or solvent wipe, hand-scuff or taber-style abrasion, and scanner verification after each step. Test on the actual container, at the actual application temperature.

Step 6: Document and lock the spec

Record facestock, adhesive, topcoat, and print profile, then enforce it in your label management workflow so a paper stock cannot quietly substitute for an approved film.

Choose paper if

The label lives indoors in dry ambient conditions, service life is short, the surface is corrugated or fibrous, cost per label dominates, and there is no wash-down, freezer, chemical, or outdoor exposure.

Choose film if

The product enters a freezer or cooler, sees condensation cycling, gets washed down or wiped with cleaners, contacts solvents or oils, is handled frequently or returned, stores outdoors, or must scan reliably for months to years.

On cost framing: film runs meaningfully more per label than paper, and the premium varies with size, construction, and volume. Weigh that premium against relabeling labor, a held or rejected shipment, and the administrative cost of closing a traceability gap. In practice, avoiding a single rejected load can offset a substantial share of a substrate upgrade on the affected SKU.

What Digital Inkjet Printing Does Differently for Paper vs. Film Substrates

Paper and film behave differently at the printhead, not just in the field — porous paper absorbs ink, while non-porous film cannot.

Porous paper ink absorption

Paper absorbs aqueous ink and dries largely by penetration into the fiber matrix, which is part of why an aqueous pigment press is a natural fit for paper-forward label runs.

Non-porous film ink requirements

Films cannot absorb anything, so they need a receptive topcoat, a compatible ink chemistry, or both, plus more dwell time or pinning and curing energy to set the image. UV-curable ink systems polymerize on contact instead of soaking in, which is why a hybrid UV press is built to run film, foil, and synthetic stocks directly.

Operational effects to plan for:

Color profiles differ by substrate

Expect separate ICC profiles and ink laydown limits for paper, white BOPP, and clear film.

Dry time and blocking risk

Under-dried film can block on the rewind, so slower speeds or added drying capacity may be required.

Static and tension

Films build static and respond differently to web tension than paper, so handling and rewind settings usually need adjustment.

Inline finishing

Lamination adhesion, die-cut depth, and matrix removal all change with facestock stiffness and liner choice.

On-demand digital label printing lets you run the correct substrate per SKU in the quantity you need, instead of buying long conventional runs of one compromise material — connecting production schedule data, artwork version control, and approved substrate specs so the right material and the current revision run together.

ArrowJet Systems for Mixed Paper and Film Label Portfolios

Mixed paper and film portfolios need a press built for variable data, short runs, and inline finishing across substrate types.

ArrowJet Aqua 330R for paper-forward and Nestlé-guidance-compliant portfolios

The ArrowJet Aqua 330R is a Memjet DuraFlex®-powered aqueous pigment press running at 90/150/195 ft/min across a max media width of 380mm on three-phase 220V/400V power. It is Nestlé Guidance Compliant across food and beverage, cosmetics, pharmaceutical, nutraceutical/supplement, and flexible packaging verticals — the portfolio breadth a mixed paper-and-treated-film label program needs from a single press.

ArrowJet UV 330H for film, foil, and durability-driven SKUs

The ArrowJet UV 330H is a true hybrid UV label press combining roll-to-roll and flatbed printing in one platform, with CMYK plus White and Varnish ink configurations. Because UV ink cures on contact instead of soaking in, the UV 330H handles films, foils, and specialty stocks that need built-in scratch and chemical resistance without an added topcoat step.

When matching any system to your substrate portfolio, confirm ink and topcoat compatibility across your material list, drying capacity at your target speeds, web handling for both paper and film, changeover behavior between substrates, and how substrate and version data flow in from your production planning tools.

Next Step: Operational Takeaways Before Your Next Material Order

Specify by environment and service life first, then price the substrate — and lock the approved spec into your label workflow.

  • Specify by environment and service life first; price the substrate after the conditions are documented.
  • Treat facestock, adhesive, and topcoat as one system, and re-qualify the set whenever one element changes.
  • Keep paper where conditions are dry, indoor, short-lived, and fibrous; move to film for freezer, condensation, wash-down, solvent, abrasion, and outdoor exposure.
  • Pre-qualify on the actual container at the actual application temperature, and verify scans after each test step.
  • Lock the approved spec into your label workflow so substitutions cannot happen quietly.

Frequently Asked Questions — Paper vs. Film Labels

Common questions from operations, engineering, QA, and packaging teams choosing between paper and film label substrates.

Are film labels always better than paper for cold storage?

Not automatically. Film removes the fiber-saturation problem, but cold-chain performance depends heavily on the adhesive and the application conditions. A film facestock with a general-purpose adhesive can still edge-lift on a frozen surface. Pair a film facestock with an all-temp or freezer-grade adhesive, and confirm the application temperature, because labels applied to already-frozen packaging behave differently than labels applied warm and then frozen. Freeze and thaw cycling on your actual container is the reliable way to know.

Can paper labels work in refrigerated, not frozen, environments?

Sometimes, with qualification. Refrigerated conditions are less severe than frozen, but condensation is often worse because product cycles between cooler and ambient. A coated or laminated paper with a suitable adhesive may hold on a dry, stable surface with a short service life. Paper tends to struggle where product is iced, hosed, or repeatedly cycled. If a barcode has to scan at multiple downstream points, film is the lower-risk choice.

How do I know if my label failure is a facestock problem or an adhesive problem?

Look at where the failure occurred. Wrinkling, tearing, softening, ink smear, fading, or scuffed print point to the facestock or topcoat. Clean lift at the edges, sliding, tunneling, or the label coming off intact with residue behind it points to the adhesive or the surface prep. Also check whether the label is still readable, because a label that stayed bonded but became unscannable is a print protection issue, not a bond issue.

Do film labels cost significantly more than paper?

Film generally costs more per label than paper, with polyester typically the highest and BOPP closer to the middle. The premium varies with size, construction, and volume, so treat any published multiple as illustrative rather than a rule. The more useful comparison is total labeling cost: material plus relabeling labor, held or rejected shipments, and complaint handling. Many teams use film only on the SKUs and environments that need it and keep paper where conditions are genuinely benign.

content.rendered:
Table of Contents

In-House Label Printing vs. Print on Demand: Cost by Volume

In-house label printing vs. print on demand comes down to a cost-per-label question: compare your fully loaded in-house cost to the outsourced landed cost at your real volume.

In-house label printing beats print-on-demand once fully loaded in-house cost per label — substrate, ink, labor, maintenance, and equipment amortization, divided by realistic annual volume — falls below the outsourced converter’s landed cost per label, which includes freight, expedite fees, obsolescence write-offs, and inventory carrying cost most quotes leave out. Crossover is a range, not a single number: SKU count and revision frequency often move it more than raw volume, because both inflate MOQ overbuy and obsolescence on the outsourced side. Most high-mix operations land on a hybrid split — short-run, high-revision, variable-data SKUs in-house on a compact industrial digital label press, long-run and specialty-decoration SKUs kept with an outsourced converter. Build both formulas with your own rates before deciding; the figures in this guide are illustrative placeholders.

Key Takeaways

  • Normalize both sides before comparing: outsourced landed cost per label versus fully loaded in-house cost per label — not a POD quote against equipment sticker price.
  • Divide by labels applied, not labels purchased. That single denominator change is what exposes MOQ overbuy and obsolescence write-offs hiding inside a POD quote.
  • SKU count and revision frequency often move the crossover volume more than raw annual volume does, because both drive overbuy and obsolescence on the outsourced side.
  • A compact, single-phase industrial press such as the ArrowJet Eco 330R lowers the volume at which in-house production stops looking like a stretch and starts looking like the obvious step up from desktop printers.
  • Finishing — laminating, die-cutting or laser-cutting, slitting, and rewinding — is half the production system; a press without matched finishing does not produce a finished roll.
  • Most high-mix plants land on a hybrid split: short-run, high-revision, variable-data SKUs in-house; long-run, stable, specialty-decoration SKUs with an outsourced converter.

How Print-on-Demand Label Services Work

POD pricing is tiered by quantity, but the quoted price excludes freight, overbuy, and obsolescence costs you absorb internally.

Quoting mechanics

Print on demand label printing cost is typically quoted in tiers by quantity, with a per-SKU minimum order. Depending on the process, you may also see one-time setup, plate, or die charges — digital runs often avoid plates but still carry setup and tooling for the cutting step. Because pricing improves at higher tiers, buyers frequently order past actual demand to reach a better break.

Typical workflow

Artwork submission, prepress review, digital or physical proof, approval, production queue, print, finishing, QC, freight, then dock receipt and put-away. Each handoff adds elapsed time, and most of that time is queue time rather than press time.

Where lead time and cost actually accumulate

Proof cycles are the most common source of slippage, especially when regulatory or brand review adds a round trip. Queue position, freight transit, and receiving inspection consume the rest. Print on demand label turnaround is rarely limited by how fast the press runs.

The quoted price per label also excludes several costs you absorb internally:

  • MOQ overbuy on SKUs that will never consume the minimum
  • Obsolescence write-offs when artwork or regulatory content is revised
  • Freight on every replenishment, plus expedite fees on rush orders
  • Inventory carrying cost — space, handling, and capital tied up in label rolls
  • Internal PO and receiving labor for each purchase transaction

How In-House Digital Label Production Works

In-house production spans prepress, RIP and color management, press and finishing, and inspection — plus real operating requirements.

Prepress and version control

Artwork is normalized to press-ready files with defined bleeds, barcodes, and variable-data fields. Version control is the discipline that makes in-house printing pay off: one approved master per SKU, with revision history and a documented release step. Regulated label content should still route through your internal quality or regulatory review before release.

RIP and color management

The RIP drives the press and applies profiles for each substrate. Repeatable brand color across runs and substrates requires calibrated profiles and periodic verification, not just a capable printer.

Press and finishing

A digital label printer (inkjet or toner) prints the web. Finishing then applies laminate or varnish, cuts the shape by rotary die or laser, slits to width, and rewinds to spec with the correct core and wind direction. Finishing capability — not print capability — is usually what limits format flexibility.

Inspection and handoff

Operators verify barcode grade, copy accuracy against the approved version, and roll construction before the roll moves to the application line.

Honest requirements

In-house production needs a trained operator, consumable inventory management, floor space for press and finishing, scheduled maintenance, and realistic uptime assumptions. Uptime, waste rate, and operator skill are the three variables that most often break an optimistic model. For teams sizing that first press, a compact, single-phase inkjet label press such as the ArrowJet Eco 330R — no air compressor required — is built specifically to keep these floor-space and utility requirements modest while still delivering true industrial single-pass output.

Per-Label Cost Comparison at Different Volume Levels

Two formulas — one for outsourced landed cost, one for in-house fully loaded cost — reveal where the real crossover volume sits.

Outsourced landed cost per label

(Quoted price × labels purchased) + freight + expedite fees + obsolescence write-off + inventory carrying cost + PO/receiving labor, divided by labels actually applied. Watch the denominator: labels applied, not labels purchased. That single change is what exposes MOQ overbuy and obsolescence.

In-house fully loaded cost per label

Substrate + ink or toner + finishing consumables (laminate, die or laser, cores) + (direct labor per hour ÷ labels per hour) + maintenance or service contract ÷ annual volume + waste and setup scrap + equipment amortization ÷ annual volume.

Inputs to collect before you decide:

  • Annual label volume (applied, not purchased)
  • Labels per SKU per order and current tier breaks
  • Active SKU count, plus expected SKU growth
  • Revisions per SKU per year
  • Average quoted lead time and actual delivered lead time
  • Expedite frequency and average expedite premium
  • Obsolescence rate — labels scrapped or written off
  • Current landed cost per label by SKU family
  • Available labor hours and shift coverage
  • Floor space for press, finishing, and consumables
  • Substrate and format mix, including any specialty decoration

Control, Turnaround, and Version Flexibility: Where In-House Wins

Same-day turnaround, single-version inventory, and late-stage variable data are where in-house production earns its keep.

Turnaround in hours instead of days

With prepress and finishing under one roof, a roll can be produced the same day it is needed. That removes expedite fees and the short-shipping scramble during launches.

Only the current version prints

There is no pre-printed inventory to reconcile against a revision. When a panel changes, the next roll reflects it, which structurally shrinks the obsolescence line in the POD formula.

Late-stage variable data

Lot codes, dates, promotional versions, and regional or language variants can be applied at print time instead of planned months ahead. High-mix operations often find this is the real value, not the unit cost.

Short-run, pilot, private-label, and co-pack SKUs

Any SKU that cannot consume a supplier’s minimum order is a candidate. Contract packagers running dozens of client artworks feel this most acutely.

Operations automation

The larger gain arrives when label production is triggered from the production schedule or ERP: the run releases, the label job releases with it, and rolls are made just in time for that order. Labeling stops being a procurement lead-time risk and becomes a scheduled production step.

When Print-on-Demand Still Makes Sense

Outsourcing still wins for low stable volume, long product lifecycles, specialty substrates, and seasonal surge capacity.

Outsourcing remains the better answer in several legitimate scenarios:

  • Low, stable volume with few SKUs. If amortization and labor per label stay high because the press would sit idle, an outsourced converter wins on math alone.
  • Long product lifecycles and infrequent revisions. Stable artwork means little obsolescence exposure, so the biggest hidden POD cost largely disappears.
  • Specialty substrates and decoration outside your range. Shrink sleeves, cold foil, specialty embellishment, and unusual formats are common POD limitations to work around — and also good reasons to keep a converter in the mix.
  • Capital constraints. When capital is committed elsewhere, paying per label converts a fixed cost into a variable one.
  • Seasonal surge capacity. Peaks that exceed in-house throughput are cheaper to buy than to buy equipment for.
  • Business continuity. Keeping a qualified outside source active protects you during maintenance windows and unplanned downtime.

The Label Press Crossover Volume — When Buying a Press Beats Paying Per Label

Crossover is a range, not a single number — compute both cost formulas, compare them, then stress-test the assumptions.

Knowing when to buy a label press starts with computing both formulas at your real volume, then comparing where they meet.

Step-by-step method:

Step 1: Compute blended POD landed cost per label

Use labels applied as the denominator, not labels purchased.

Step 2: Compute fully loaded in-house cost per label

Use your realistic annual volume: realistic uptime, realistic throughput, realistic waste rate — not the vendor’s best-case numbers.

Step 3: Compare the two, then solve for the volume at which they converge

That convergence point is your crossover volume.

Step 4: Re-run the model at several volumes

This shows how wide the indifference band is around your crossover point.

Sensitivity tests to run, at minimum:

  • Volume ±30% — the single largest driver of amortization per label
  • Direct labor rate and shift coverage
  • Uptime assumption (model 70–85% rather than 100%; illustrative range only)
  • Waste and setup scrap rate
  • SKU growth over 24–36 months
  • Revisions per SKU per year

Crossover is a range, not a single number. Every input above moves it. In practice, SKU count and revision frequency often move crossover more than raw volume, because they drive MOQ overbuy and obsolescence on the outsourced side while adding only setup time in-house. Two plants with identical annual volume can land on opposite sides of the line.

Recommended hybrid split. Most mid-market operations do better with a hybrid label printing model than with picking just one approach. Run high-mix, short-run, high-revision, and variable-data SKUs in-house, where turnaround and version control matter most — on a press and finishing line sized to that mix, such as an entry-level digital press paired with the Arrow EZCut 330R+ blade die cutter for standard shapes and the ArrowCut Nova 330R laser finisher for short-run or custom-shape jobs. Keep long-run, stable, and specialty-decoration SKUs with an outsourced converter, where tier pricing and process capability win.

Decision traps to avoid:

  • Comparing a POD quote against equipment cost only, with no labor, consumables, or waste
  • Ignoring finishing — print without cutting and rewinding is not a finished roll
  • Assuming zero setup scrap and 100% uptime
  • Building the model on a peak month instead of annual volume
  • Using labels purchased rather than labels applied as the denominator

Frequently Asked Questions — In-House vs. Print-on-Demand Label Printing

Common questions from operations, packaging, and procurement leads comparing in-house label production to print-on-demand.

What volume makes in-house label printing worth it?

There is no universal threshold. Build both formulas with your own rates, then find where fully loaded in-house cost meets blended outsourced landed cost. Plants with many SKUs and frequent revisions often reach that point at lower volumes than expected, because MOQ overbuy and obsolescence inflate the outsourced side well beyond the quoted price.

How does print-on-demand label turnaround compare to in-house?

Outsourced turnaround is usually measured in days to weeks, driven mostly by proof cycles, queue position, and freight rather than press time. In-house production is typically measured in hours once prepress is approved and consumables are on hand. Actual timing depends on your approval workflow, staffing, and finishing capacity.

Can we run a hybrid model with both?

Yes, and it is often the strongest answer. Segment the portfolio by run length, revision frequency, and decoration requirements. Keep long-run and specialty SKUs with a converter, and bring short-run, high-revision, and variable-data SKUs in-house. The hybrid also preserves an outside source as backup capacity during maintenance or demand spikes.

Next Step

Pull twelve months of label spend, SKU count, and lead time first — that’s roughly 80% of the crossover model.

Run your own numbers first. Pull your last 12 months of label spend, active SKU count, revisions per SKU, and average lead time — that is roughly 80% of the model, and it will tell you quickly whether this is worth pursuing. Plug those figures into the in-house label printing cost formula above and compare it to your blended outsourced landed cost.

Operational takeaways:

  • Normalize both sides before comparing: outsourced landed cost versus fully loaded in-house cost.
  • Divide by labels applied, not labels purchased, so overbuy and obsolescence show up.
  • Model realistic uptime, throughput, and scrap; optimistic assumptions move crossover the most.
  • Treat crossover as a range, and test volume, labor, SKU growth, and revision frequency against it.
  • Expect a hybrid split: short-run and high-revision SKUs in-house, long-run and specialty SKUs outsourced.

Results depend on your actual volumes, rates, and mix; no savings or payback outcome is guaranteed. Arrow Systems manufactures digital label printing and finishing equipment; Arrow does not print or supply labels on a customer’s behalf.
